Calculate thermal resistance: theta-JC = (Tj - Tcase) / Pdiss, where Tcase is measured by thermocouple on the package. theta-JA = (Tj - Tambient) / Pdiss. Compare measured values to the datasheet. If measured theta-JA is higher than the datasheet value, the board thermal design is worse than the datasheet test condition (usually a JEDEC standard test board with specific copper area).

Assess derating: most semiconductor reliability guidelines recommend operating at least 20-30C below the rated maximum junction temperature. For components running near the limit, calculate the temperature rise above ambient and identify the thermal path improvement needed (more copper, thermal vias, heat sink, improved airflow) to achieve adequate margin.

description: Conduct systematic failure analysis of electronic assemblies from initial electrical characterization through non-destructive and destructive inspection to root cause determination and corrective action.

steps.description: Reproduce the reported failure, characterize the electrical symptoms, and narrow the fault to a specific circuit or component through systematic measurement before any physical inspection.

inputs.name: failure-report
inputs.desc: Description of the failure: symptoms, conditions, intermittent vs permanent, field or manufacturing origin

inputs.name: board-documentation
inputs.desc: Schematic, layout, BOM, and any available production test data for the failed unit

outputs.name: failure-reproduction
outputs.desc: Confirmed failure mode with the conditions required to reproduce it (temperature, load, timing, sequence)

outputs.name: electrical-characterization
outputs.desc: Measured electrical parameters that deviate from specification, with comparison to a known-good reference unit

outputs.name: fault-localization
outputs.desc: Suspected component or circuit area based on electrical measurements, narrowed to the minimum ambiguity group

process: Review the failure report for context: field return (usage conditions, age, environment) or manufacturing fallout (which test step caught it, what the test data shows). If production test data is available, analyze the parametric trend for this unit compared to the population (was it marginal at test or a sudden failure?).

Attempt to reproduce the failure under controlled conditions. If the failure is intermittent, systematically vary temperature (hot and cold), voltage (high and low line), mechanical stress (board flex, connector reseat), and timing (power sequencing, data rate) to find the conditions that trigger it. Document the exact conditions for reproducibility.

Compare the failed unit to a known-good reference unit. Measure power supply voltages, clock frequencies, signal amplitudes, and communication waveforms on both units under identical conditions. The difference between good and failed unit measurements points to the fault area.

Use divide-and-conquer to narrow the fault. For a signal chain failure, probe the signal at intermediate points between input and output. The last point where the signal is good and the first point where it is bad brackets the faulty component. For power supply failures, measure upstream to downstream until the fault is located.

For intermittent failures that cannot be reproduced on the bench, apply environmental stress (thermal chamber, vibration) while monitoring the symptomatic signal on an oscilloscope with a persistence or envelope capture mode. The intermittent event will eventually appear and the environmental condition at the moment of failure provides a clue to the mechanism.

steps.description: Inspect the failed assembly using non-destructive methods including visual inspection, X-ray, acoustic microscopy, and dye penetrant to identify physical defects without altering the evidence.

inputs.name: fault-localization
inputs.desc: Suspected component or area from electrical characterization

inputs.name: electrical-characterization
inputs.desc: Measured deviations to correlate with physical findings

outputs.name: visual-inspection-findings
outputs.desc: Optical and stereo microscope observations: solder joint appearance, component damage, PCB defects, contamination

outputs.name: xray-inspection-results
outputs.desc: X-ray images of suspect solder joints showing voids, bridging, head-in-pillow, and other hidden defects under BGA and QFN packages

outputs.name: non-destructive-diagnosis
outputs.desc: Preliminary failure mechanism hypothesis based on non-destructive evidence, with confidence assessment

process: Start with unaided visual inspection: look for obvious physical damage, discoloration (burn marks, heat damage), cracked components, bent pins, contamination, or corrosion. Photograph everything before handling. Handle the board by the edges with ESD-safe gloves to preserve contamination evidence.

Move to stereo microscope inspection (10x to 45x magnification) of the suspect area. Examine solder joints for cold solder (grainy, dull finish), insufficient solder, excess solder, solder bridges, lifted pads, cracked joints, or tin whiskers. For through-hole components, check for solder fill (barrel fill should be 75% minimum per IPC-A-610).

For BGA, QFN, and other hidden-joint packages, use X-ray inspection. In 2D X-ray, look for: voids (dark circles in solder balls, acceptable up to 25% of ball area per IPC-7095), bridging (solder connecting adjacent balls), head-in-pillow (ball and pad solder did not fully merge, showing a distinct boundary), and missing or misaligned balls. If available, use 3D X-ray (CT) to see the joint profile in cross-section without cutting.

For suspected delamination or die-attach voids, use scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM/C-SAM). Acoustic imaging reveals voids and delamination at interfaces (die to die-attach, die-attach to leadframe, board layer delamination) that are invisible to X-ray. Voids appear as bright (high reflection) areas at the interface.

Correlate non-destructive findings with electrical symptoms. A void in a BGA solder ball correlates with an intermittent open. A solder bridge matches a short between two nets. Die-attach voiding correlates with thermal failure (hot spot on the die from poor heat conduction). If the non-destructive evidence is conclusive, document it and proceed to root cause. If inconclusive, proceed to destructive analysis.

steps.description: Perform destructive physical analysis including cross-sectioning, SEM/EDS, and dye-and-pry to determine the failure mechanism at the microstructural level.

inputs.name: non-destructive-diagnosis
inputs.desc: Hypothesis and evidence from non-destructive inspection

inputs.name: fault-localization
inputs.desc: Specific component or joint to section

outputs.name: cross-section-results
outputs.desc: Metallographic cross-section images showing solder joint microstructure, intermetallic thickness, crack path, and void morphology

outputs.name: material-analysis
outputs.desc: EDS (Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy) composition analysis at failure site identifying contaminants, corrosion products, or unexpected materials

outputs.name: failure-mechanism-determination
outputs.desc: Root cause identification: failure mechanism (fatigue, overstress, contamination, EOS/ESD, manufacturing defect) with supporting evidence from the physical analysis

process: For solder joint analysis, use dye-and-pry first (for BGA/CSP). Apply fluorescent dye to the suspect area, allow it to wick into any cracks. Remove the component by heating above solder liquidus and lifting off. Examine the fracture surfaces under UV light: dye penetration marks the pre-existing crack; fresh fracture surfaces (from removal) are dye-free. This reveals the crack location (board side, component side, bulk solder, intermetallic) and extent.

Cross-section the suspect joint or component. Mount the sample in epoxy, grind and polish through the target plane using progressively finer abrasive (180 grit to 0.05um alumina). Etch the polished surface to reveal grain boundaries if needed (for solder: 5% HCl in methanol for 5 seconds). Examine under optical microscope at 50x to 500x.

Examine the cross-section for failure signatures. Thermal fatigue: intergranular crack propagating from the stress concentration point (package corner for BGA), with grain coarsening near the crack. Mechanical overstress: transgranular crack with little deformation. Solder void: smooth spherical cavity in the joint interior. Kirkendall voiding: line of voids at the Cu-Sn intermetallic interface from diffusion imbalance (indicates excessive thermal exposure).

Use SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) for high-magnification imaging of the fracture surface or cross-section. EDS (Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy) identifies elemental composition: detect tin whiskers (pure Sn), contamination (Cl, S for corrosion; Na, K for flux residue), intermetallic composition (Cu6Sn5 vs Cu3Sn), and foreign material.

Determine the root cause category: design (thermal stress exceeds joint fatigue life, inadequate pad size), component (internal defect, incoming quality issue), process (reflow profile, paste deposit volume, placement accuracy, cleanliness), or field stress (thermal cycling, mechanical shock, corrosion from environment). Document the evidence chain from symptom to mechanism to root cause.

steps.description: Define corrective actions from the root cause, verify their effectiveness, document the complete failure analysis, and analyze field return trends for systemic issues.

inputs.name: failure-mechanism-determination
inputs.desc: Confirmed root cause with evidence

inputs.name: failure-report
inputs.desc: Original failure context for trend analysis

outputs.name: corrective-action-plan
outputs.desc: Specific corrective actions addressing the root cause: design change, process parameter adjustment, or component change, with owner and timeline

outputs.name: failure-analysis-report
outputs.desc: Complete FA report: failure description, analysis sequence, evidence at each step, root cause, corrective action, and lessons learned

outputs.name: trend-analysis
outputs.desc: Comparison of this failure mode to historical field returns and manufacturing fallout data, identifying if it is a new mode or a recurring pattern

process: Define corrective actions matched to the root cause category. For design root cause: modify the design (pad size, trace routing, thermal relief, component selection) and verify with analysis or prototype. For process root cause: adjust the process parameter (reflow profile, stencil aperture, placement force) and run a process validation (DOE or first-article inspection). For component root cause: escalate to the component supplier with evidence and qualification data.

Verify corrective action effectiveness. For design changes, run accelerated life testing on the modified design. For process changes, monitor the affected measurement on the next production lot. Define the success criteria: zero recurrence of this failure mode for N units, or parametric shift below a threshold.

Write the failure analysis report. Structure: executive summary (one paragraph with root cause and action), failure description and context, analysis sequence (each step with images and data), root cause determination (evidence chain), corrective action and verification plan, and lessons learned. Include all images at sufficient resolution for peer review.

Analyze the failure against the historical database. Is this failure mode new or recurring? If recurring, the prior corrective action was ineffective and needs escalation. Calculate the failure rate for this mode: failures per million units per year (or per thousand power-on-hours). Compare to the reliability prediction for this failure mode to assess whether the actual failure rate exceeds the predicted rate.

Feed the findings back to design and manufacturing. Add this failure mode to the FMEA for the product family. Update the incoming inspection criteria if the root cause was a component defect. Update the functional test limits if the test missed a precursor signature that could have caught this failure at production test.
